title: US wait times for cancer surgeries are increasing, impacting patient outcomes
summary: A study published in JAMA Surgery reveals that wait times for cancer surgeries in the US have significantly increased from 2012 to 2023 for six types of cancer: breast, colon, lung, pancreatic, gastric, and esophageal. The delays, linked to poorer outcomes and increased patient distress, disproportionately affect socioeconomically vulnerable groups, including uninsured or Medicaid patients, Black patients, lower-income individuals, and those traveling longer distances for treatment. The trend coincides with healthcare system consolidation, raising concerns about patient bottlenecks at centralized, high-volume treatment centers.
key_points: Wait times for cancer surgeries in the US have increased across six cancer types (breast, colon, lung, pancreatic, gastric, esophageal) from 2012 to 2023.
Delays are associated with poorer outcomes, including reduced survival rates and increased patient anxiety.
The study analyzed data from over 2.7 million patients with non-metastatic stage I–III cancers requiring surgery.
Wait times rose incrementally across four time periods: 2012–2015, 2016–2019, 2020–2021, and 2022–2023.
Proportions of patients experiencing prolonged waits (30+ days) and extreme waits (60+ days) also increased.
Healthcare system consolidation and centralization may contribute to bottlenecks at high-volume treatment centers.
Socioeconomically vulnerable groups, such as uninsured/Medicaid patients, Black patients, lower-income individuals, and those with longer travel distances, face disproportionately longer wait times.
Researchers suggest optimizing scheduling, increasing capacity at centralized centers, and selectively referring complex cases to mitigate delays.
